analysis.title: US retail sales and manufacturing suggest strong momentum
key_insights: October US retail sales rose 0.2% MoM versus 0.1% consensus. The control group (excludes gasoline, autos, building materials and restaurants) rose 0.6% MoM versus 0.3% expected, and September was revised up 0.4pp to 0.5% MoM.

The retail sales figures are nominal. Hotter-than-expected October inflation leaves headline sales negative in real terms and core activity flat to slightly higher, implying a smaller consumer contribution to 4Q GDP growth than in 3Q.

Most of the October retail strength came from the miscellaneous store category, up 4.7% MoM after a 3% fall in September. Gasoline stations and health and personal care were each up 1.5%, and non-store/internet was up 1.2%.
Furniture (-2.3%), autos (-1.6%), clothing (-0.7%) and sporting goods (-0.7%) declined in October.

Retail sales are a shrinking share of total consumer spending. Middle and lower income households face wage growth below the rising cost of living and spend more on goods. High income households, helped by wealth gains, spend more on services that retail sales exclude, so non-retail spending is expected to keep outperforming.
October industrial production fell 0.4% MoM versus +0.1% consensus. The miss came from a 4.3% drop in utilities output on mild weather. Mining fell 0.8%.

Manufacturing output rose 0.3% MoM in October. Business equipment rose 1%, defence and space 0.9%, motor vehicles and parts 4.4%, and computer and electronic products 1.4%. Aircraft, electrical equipment, appliances and fabricated metal products were weak.

October ISM manufacturing rose to 55.5 from 54.5 in September. Manufacturers added 101,000 jobs year-to-date after three years of declines, and average weekly hours rose 30 minutes to 40.5 versus a year ago.
ING attributes the manufacturing gains to tech capex, tariffs, US energy security with low energy costs (helping steel and glass), and US growth outperforming other major markets.

ING expects high value-added manufacturing (tech, electronics, transport, power-related) to keep outperforming on strong tech investment pipelines. Traditional, labour-intensive, commoditised manufacturing will keep shrinking, since tariffs do not offset high US production costs and retaliatory tariffs hurt these producers abroad.

sector_views.rationale: Strong pipelines for tech-related investment, low energy costs and US growth support continued outperformance.
Tariffs do not offset the high cost of US production, and retaliatory tariffs hurt these producers in foreign markets.
Control group is strong, but real sales are weak and lower and middle income households are squeezed, while spending shifts toward services.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Slight beat on a nominal basis, but negative in real terms after higher inflation.

tension_points.bull_case: Control group rose 0.6% MoM versus 0.3% expected, with September revised up to 0.5%, and high income households are boosting consumption.
tension_points.bear_case: The figures are nominal, so real headline sales are negative and core flat to slightly higher. Middle and lower income households are squeezed by wages lagging living costs, and October strength was concentrated in the volatile miscellaneous category.
